channel.title: Study on Best of AI
channel.description: Recent content in Study on Best of AI

item.title: 360Learning
item.description:
360Learning is based on the idea that the people who know a topic best are usually inside the company, not in a training department. Experts build short courses with the platform’s authoring tool, colleagues give feedback in comments, and learners can ask questions that feed back into the material. It is called collaborative learning.

The platform covers the usual LMS functions: assigning training, tracking completion, compliance, and reporting. Learning paths and skills features help manage development, and integrations connect with HR and communication tools. An AI assistant generates outlines, lessons, and quiz questions from documents, which reduces the time needed to create content.

item.title: Adobe Captivate
item.description:
Captivate is a long-standing tool for instructional designers. They build courses from slides with interactive elements like quizzes, branching scenarios, drag and drop exercises, and video. A standout feature is software simulation, where the tool records on-screen steps in an application and turns them into demonstrations or practice exercises, which helps train employees on new systems.

Courses are responsive, so they work on desktops and mobile devices, and they publish in formats that learning management systems can track, including SCORM, xAPI, and HTML5. Assets from Adobe’s other tools can be reused. Recent versions add AI help, such as text to speech for narration and automatic generation of some content.

item.title: Brainly
item.description:
Brainly grew from a Q&A site for students. A learner posts a question, other users and moderators answer it, and the best responses are verified. Over time, it has built a large library of questions and answers across math, science, languages, and history, with versions for many countries that follow local curricula.

The product now blends community with AI. An AI tutor gives step-by-step explanations, can solve problems from a photo, and helps with writing and study guides. A paid plan removes ads and unlocks more AI help and expert-verified answers. Some features are free with limits.

item.title: Cornerstone OnDemand
item.description:
Cornerstone OnDemand is one of the established vendors of learning management systems. Large employers use it to host training, assign compliance courses, track completion, and manage development plans. The platform covers learning, performance reviews, succession planning, and a content library from outside providers.

Its newer direction centers on skills. AI infers the skills employees have from their roles and activity, compares them to what jobs require, and recommends courses and career paths. Generative AI helps create content, summarize learning, and give managers guidance. The aim is to move from course catalogs to skill growth.

item.title: Course Hero
item.description:
Course Hero started as a library of materials uploaded by students from their classes. Learners search for notes, practice problems, and study guides tied to specific courses and schools, and unlock documents by uploading their own or paying for a subscription. Tutors answer questions on a range of subjects.

An AI assistant now sits alongside the library. It explains concepts, helps with study guides and flashcards, and answers questions about uploaded materials. This makes the site more of a general study tool than a document repository, though the document library remains the main draw for many users.

item.title: DataCamp
item.description:
DataCamp is built around learning by doing. Each lesson combines a few minutes of video with exercises you complete in an in-browser editor, so you write real code with immediate feedback and no setup. Courses cover Python, R, SQL, Excel, Power BI, statistics, machine learning, and more recently AI and large language models, taught by instructors from industry and academia.

Structured paths help learners progress. Career tracks, such as data analyst or data scientist, string together courses and projects, skill assessments show strengths and gaps, and certifications validate skills for employers. An AI assistant gives hints and explains errors, and a workspace allows practice in notebooks. Teams can buy it for corporate training with reporting.

item.title: MagicSchool
item.description:
MagicSchool was built for educators. Teachers choose a tool, such as a lesson plan generator, rubric builder, quiz maker, IEP helper, or email writer, fill in a short form, and receive a draft they can edit. More than eighty tools cover planning, assessment, communication, and support for students with different needs, which saves time on routine paperwork.

Student-facing features let teachers create safe AI chat rooms for classes, where they set the topic, rules, and level of help, and see the conversations. The platform emphasizes privacy and compliance for schools, with settings designed to protect students, and districts can adopt it with administrative controls. Integrations connect with Google Classroom and other learning tools.

item.title: Photomath
item.description:
Photomath makes it easy to get unstuck on math. You point your phone’s camera at a printed or handwritten problem, and the app recognizes it and shows the answer along with steps for solving it. It covers arithmetic, algebra, geometry, trigonometry, and calculus, and explains the reasoning for each step, so students can learn the method instead of copying an answer.

Further features support learning. Animated tutorials illustrate how steps work, multiple solution methods are available for some problems, and a graphing tool shows functions. Recent versions add AI-powered explanations that answer follow-up questions, and the app works in many languages. Teachers and parents use it to check work and see how a problem can be approached.

item.title: Quizgecko
item.description:
Quizgecko speeds up quiz writing. A user pastes text, uploads a file, or links to a page, chooses a question type and difficulty, and the AI generates a set of questions with answers. Quizzes can be edited, shared with a link, embedded, or exported to learning platforms.

Teachers use it for classroom quizzes and practice tests, trainers for compliance checks, and students for self-testing. Flashcards and other study formats are available, and analytics show how learners performed.

item.title: Scholé
item.description:
Scholé rethinks workplace learning. Instead of asking employees to finish courses on the side, it delivers short, relevant learning moments tied to real tasks, adapting to what a person already knows and needs to do. Principles from learning science, such as practice and spaced repetition, shape the design.

Teams can use it to build skills in areas like communication, sales, or technical topics, with AI creating content and feedback. The idea is learning that fits into work and sticks.

item.title: QuillBotAI Pro: Free AI Content Detector for Educators & Publishers
item.description:
QuillBotAI Pro offers a web tool where a user pastes text and receives a score estimating how likely it is to be machine written. It advertises detection of output from several major models, including text that has been rewritten to avoid detection, and positions the service as free and unlimited.

Educators and publishers use detectors as a first screen. Detection is inherently unreliable: tools produce false positives, especially on writing by non-native English speakers, and can miss edited AI text. A score should start a conversation, not decide a case.

item.title: Docebo
item.description:
Docebo is a cloud learning platform for businesses. Administrators host courses, assign training, track completion, and report on results for employees, customers, and partners. Enterprises use it for onboarding, compliance training, and external education that supports product adoption.

AI is built throughout. It automatically tags content, recommends courses to learners by role and interests, and can generate lessons, quizzes, and summaries from documents and videos. A skills layer maps what learners know to what roles need. A content marketplace provides courses from outside providers.

item.title: Articulate 360
item.description:
Articulate 360 is a suite for creating online training. Storyline is a slide-based tool for custom interactions, branching scenarios, and simulations, while Rise builds responsive, web-style courses quickly from blocks. Other tools in the suite handle screen recording, video, and review feedback, and a library of templates and stock media is included.

Courses export to standard formats such as SCORM and xAPI, so they work in most learning management systems. Reviewers can comment on a course through a web link, which streamlines feedback. AI Assistant helps write lesson text, quiz questions, and image ideas, speeding up the first draft.

item.title: Brilliant
item.description:
Brilliant teaches by making you work through problems. Instead of watching a lecture, you manipulate diagrams, solve puzzles, and answer questions that build up from basic ideas, with immediate feedback. Lessons are short, so it fits into a daily routine. Courses cover topics such as logic, algebra, calculus, probability, statistics, physics, computer science, programming, and, more recently, AI and machine learning concepts.

The learning path is designed to develop intuition before formal rules. It breaks big topics into small steps, uses visuals heavily, and reviews earlier material to help it stick. Adaptive features adjust difficulty based on how you do, and AI features offer hints and explanations when you get stuck. Courses are written by educators and professionals, and they are polished in a way that appeals to curious adults as well as students.

item.title: Carnegie Learning
item.description: Carnegie Learning grew out of research at Carnegie Mellon University on how people learn math. Its flagship product, MATHia, is an intelligent tutoring system that watches how a student solves each step of a problem, estimates which skills the student has mastered, and adjusts the next problem and hints accordingly. The aim is to give every student something like a personal tutor, with feedback at the moment a mistake occurs.

item.title: Chegg AI
item.description:
Chegg began by renting textbooks and grew into a subscription service for homework help. Students could search a library of solved textbook problems, ask experts questions, and get tutoring. The model worked well until general-purpose chatbots arrived, at which point many students began asking ChatGPT instead. Chegg’s traffic and subscriber numbers fell sharply, and the company has cut staff more than once and rethought its strategy.

CheggMate is the company’s response, an AI study assistant that combines large language models with Chegg’s own content. It aims to explain problems step by step, help with concepts, and generate practice questions, drawing on the study material the company has built over the years. The goal is to be more reliable for coursework than a generic chatbot because it grounds answers in verified content.

item.title: Copyleaks
item.description:
Copyleaks checks text for originality. It compares documents against web pages, publications, and its own databases to find copied passages, and it also estimates whether text was written by an AI model. Schools, publishers, and businesses use it to check student work, submissions, and content.

It supports many languages and file types, and integrates with learning management systems so teachers can scan assignments in their usual workflow. Reports show matched sources and highlight text flagged as likely AI-written. Additional tools cover code plagiarism and a writing assistant.

item.title: Coursera
item.description:
Coursera partners with universities and companies to offer online learning at scale. Learners can take individual courses, follow multi-course specializations and professional certificates from names like Google, IBM, and Meta, or enroll in full online degrees. Material combines video lectures, readings, quizzes, and graded assignments, and many courses can be audited for free. Completed programs earn certificates that people add to resumes and LinkedIn.

AI has become part of the platform. A learning assistant answers questions about course content, gives feedback, and helps with practice, and tools help instructors and organizations build and translate courses faster. Skills-based recommendations suggest what to learn next based on your goals. The platform also offers business and government offerings, where employers assign programs and track progress.

item.title: DreamBox Learning
item.description: DreamBox Math is designed to give every student lessons at the right level. As a child works through interactive, game-based problems, the software tracks not only whether answers are correct but also how the child solves them: the strategies used, the time taken, and the kinds of mistakes made. It uses that information to adjust the next activity, moving ahead when the student is ready and revisiting ideas when they are shaky.

item.title: GPTZero
item.description: GPTZero was created by a Princeton student soon after ChatGPT appeared and became one of the most used AI detectors. You paste text or upload a document, and it returns the probability that the writing is human or AI, with sentences highlighted by likelihood. It looks at features such as perplexity and burstiness, which describe how predictable and varied the writing is, and uses trained models for classification. Teachers, editors, and publishers use it to flag content for a closer look.

item.title: IXL
item.description:
IXL provides practice at scale. Students work through skills organized by grade level, and the questions get easier or harder based on their answers. Instant feedback explains mistakes, and a real-time diagnostic estimates the level at which a student is working across subjects.

Teachers and parents get reports showing progress, strengths, and gaps, and suggested next skills. The platform aligns with state standards, which helps classroom use. AI features offer personalized recommendations and help with tutoring, and the company offers add-ons such as a writing coach.

item.title: Khan Academy
item.description:
Khan Academy provides free education to anyone with an internet connection. Its library of short videos, articles, and interactive exercises covers school subjects from basic arithmetic through calculus, biology, chemistry, grammar, history, and test preparation such as the SAT. Learners can follow structured courses, and the mastery system encourages students to practice until they have a skill before moving ahead.

For teachers and schools, it offers tools to assign work, track progress, and see which students need help. District partnerships connect it with curricula, and Khan Academy Kids offers content for young children in a separate app. The nonprofit is funded by donations and philanthropic support rather than by charging learners, which sets it apart from commercial education companies.

item.title: Khanmigo
item.description:
Khanmigo is designed around a tutoring philosophy. Instead of handing students the answer, it asks guiding questions, offers hints, and checks understanding, much like a good human tutor. It works with Khan Academy’s exercises and videos, so it can step in when a student gets stuck on a particular problem. It also offers activities such as practicing a debate, writing with feedback, and exploring historical figures through role-play.

Teachers have a version with tools that save planning time. It can help create lesson plans, quizzes, rubrics, and examples, suggest ways to explain a concept, and differentiate material for different levels. Teachers can see how students interact with it, which provides insight into where they struggle. Safeguards are built in, such as moderation and notifying adults if conversations raise concerns, because the users are children.

item.title: Mathway
item.description:
Mathway helps students check and understand math. A user enters a problem or snaps a photo, and the app returns the answer and, with a subscription, the steps used to reach it. It covers algebra, trigonometry, calculus, statistics, and more.

Used well, step-by-step solutions help a student learn a method. Used carelessly, they let students copy answers without understanding, and teachers often restrict such tools. Automated solvers can also make errors, especially with word problems and unusual notation.

item.title: Quizlet AI
item.description:
Quizlet is a long-running tool for learning through flashcards. Students create or find sets of terms and definitions, then study them with modes such as flashcards, learn sessions that adapt to what you miss, matching games, and practice tests. A huge library of user-created sets covers school subjects, languages, and professional exams, and teachers use it to build class activities.

AI has added help with creating and understanding material. Tools can generate flashcards or quizzes from uploaded notes, textbook pages, or slides, saving the effort of typing each card. An AI tutor can explain a concept, quiz you, and give step-by-step help, and features track progress and suggest what to review. Study guides and summaries can be produced from your own materials.

item.title: Socratic by Google
item.description:
Socratic began as a startup and was acquired by Google, which relaunched it as a free app for students. A learner took a photo of a homework problem, and the app identified the concept and pointed to videos, explanations, and step-by-step guidance from across the web instead of just giving an answer.

It covered subjects such as math, science, and literature, and used machine learning to match questions to educational content. The goal was to help students understand a topic, not only to produce a solution.

item.title: StudySmarter
item.description:
StudySmarter helps students prepare for exams. You upload lecture notes, a PDF, or a textbook chapter, and the app generates flashcards and summaries from the content. Quizzes test what you have learned, spaced repetition schedules reviews, and a study planner breaks your exam preparation into manageable sessions. A large library of shared flashcards and notes from other students covers school and university subjects.

AI features act as a study partner. An assistant can explain concepts, answer questions, and generate practice problems, and the app can create mind maps and summaries from uploaded materials. Progress tracking shows what you know and what needs more review. The app was founded in Germany and is used in many countries, with content aligned to various curricula.

item.title: Turnitin
item.description:
Turnitin compares student submissions against a large database of papers, publications, and web content, producing a similarity report for instructors. It integrates with systems such as Canvas, Blackboard, and Moodle, so checking fits into grading.

An AI writing indicator estimates how much of a submission may be AI generated. AI detection is imperfect: false positives and negatives occur, and results are best used as a prompt for conversation, not proof. Feedback and grading tools add other functions.

item.title: Udemy
item.description:
Udemy opened online teaching to anyone. Instructors create video courses on a huge range of topics, from Python programming and UX design to photography and personal finance, and learners buy them individually, often at steep discounts. Courses can be watched at your own pace for life, and ratings and reviews help buyers choose. Quality varies widely, as there is little gatekeeping.

For companies, Udemy Business provides a curated library of courses with analytics and learning paths, which many organizations use for employee training. AI features include assistants that answer questions about course content, recommend lessons, and help instructors build courses, and role-play practice tools for skills training. Udemy has emphasized AI and technology skills, which are among its most popular categories.

item.title: Codecademy
item.description:
Codecademy teaches coding by doing. Lessons present a short explanation beside an editor where learners write code and see results right away, which makes it approachable for beginners. Courses cover languages such as Python, JavaScript, and SQL, as well as web development, data analysis, and machine learning.

Career paths and skill paths structure the learning, with projects and quizzes to check progress. An AI assistant helps learners who are stuck by giving hints and explaining errors, while avoiding simply handing over answers. Business plans let companies train teams, and Skillsoft acquired Codecademy to add it to its corporate learning catalog.

item.title: edX
item.description:
edX was founded by Harvard and MIT as a nonprofit to put university courses online. Learners can audit many courses for free or pay for verified certificates, and the catalog includes professional certificates, bootcamps, and online degree programs from partner universities and companies.

The platform later became part of 2U, a company that builds online programs with universities. edX.org remains a major destination for learners seeking credentials, and offers courses in computer science, data, business, and many other fields. Business offerings train employees. The open-source Open edX software that powers many other learning sites is separate from edX.org.

item.title: Synthesis
item.description:
Synthesis grew out of a school experiment. The idea is that children learn best by working together on puzzles, simulations, and strategic games that require reasoning, instead of by memorizing procedures. Sessions are live and collaborative: a small group of children plays through challenges guided by a facilitator, which builds skills in math, logic, teamwork, and communication.

A more recent product, the Synthesis Tutor, uses AI to give each child personalized practice. It adapts to what a child knows, presents math concepts through games and stories, and gives feedback that encourages persistence. Parents get information about progress. The program is designed for elementary and middle school ages and is used by homeschoolers and others looking for enrichment.

item.title: Thea
item.description:
Thea focuses on learning over answer-getting. A student uploads notes or a textbook section, and Thea creates questions, hints, and explanations that walk through the material step by step, asking the student to think rather than handing over the solution.

Features include quizzes, flashcards, and summaries built from the student’s own materials, which keeps study aligned with the course. The approach aligns with research showing that retrieval practice improves memory.

item.title: Vertech Academy
item.description:
Vertech Academy sells guides and templates for studying with AI. Rather than ad hoc prompting, students follow workflows for tasks such as breaking down a topic, testing themselves, and planning revision, using chat assistants.

The idea is to help learners use AI actively, as a tutor that asks questions, instead of copying answers. Structure may help those who are unsure how to begin.

Independent information is limited, and results depend on student effort. Check what is included before paying. Alternatives include Khanmigo, NotebookLM, Quizlet, and prompts shared freely by educators. Vertech Academy suits students seeking structured approaches to AI study.
